original_question: What additional invariants, recognition methods, or classification principles can distinguish the Kishino virtual knot from the unknot and clarify when a non-trivial virtual knot can arise as the connected sum of two trivial virtual knots, especially in view of the fact that connected sum is not well defined for closed virtual knots but is ordered and well defined for long virtual knots?
correct_elements: Your draft correctly identifies the paper’s main target: the Kishino knot as a paradigmatic nontrivial virtual knot that can arise as a connected sum of two trivial virtual knot diagrams, together with the key distinction that connected sum is not well defined for closed/compact virtual knots but is ordered and well defined in the long-virtual-knot category. It also correctly keeps the focus on recognition/distinguishing methods and on the related classification issue rather than drifting to broader virtual-knot problems.
missing_details: The nearest official formulation is Section 7, Problem 1, explicitly titled "Recognising the Kishino Knot," so the target is not a general search for stronger virtual-knot invariants but this specific Kishino/connected-sum problem.

The paper records five already known ways to detect Kishino’s nontriviality: the 3-strand Jones polynomial, the Ξ-polynomial, the quaternionic biquandle, the surface bracket polynomial, and Kadokami’s proof via the immersion class of a shadow curve in genus two.

The paper phrases the first part as: even though Kishino is already recognized by several methods, "other proofs of its non-triviality may be illuminating"; your draft should reflect that this is about further illuminating recognitions/proofs, not a broader classification of all possible invariants.
The second part is specifically: classify when a nontrivial virtual knot can be the connected sum of two trivial virtual knots.

The hidden reason for that classification problem is that connected sum of closed/compact virtual knots is not well defined, so different choices of connected-sum operation can produce genuinely different effects.
The paper adds one more closely related target that your draft only hints at: classify the different long virtual knots whose closures are equivalent to the unknot.

No ambient ring, coefficient field, polynomial variables, homogeneity conditions, degree restrictions, or nilpotency hypotheses belong to this problem; it is a categorical/classificatory virtual-knot problem rather than an algebraic one.
refined_question: Given that the Kishino virtual knot is already known to be nontrivial by the 3-strand Jones polynomial, the Ξ-polynomial, the quaternionic biquandle, the surface bracket polynomial, and Kadokami’s genus-two shadow-curve method, can one find further illuminating recognitions/proofs of its nontriviality and, more fundamentally, classify exactly when a nontrivial compact virtual knot can occur as a connected sum of two trivial virtual knots, taking into account that connected sum for closed virtual knots is not well defined, whereas for long virtual knots it is an ordered well-defined operation; closely relatedly, can one classify the long virtual knots whose closures are equivalent to the unknot?
justification: The draft is aiming at the paper’s Section 7, Problem 1, not at a neighboring problem. That problem explicitly starts from known ways of recognizing Kishino, asks whether further proofs would still be illuminating, and then sharpens the issue to the classification of nontrivial virtual knots that arise as connected sums of two trivial virtual knots. The surrounding Section 2 discussion supplies the essential hidden assumptions: closed/compact virtual connected sum is not well defined, long connected sum is well defined but ordered, and Kishino is the motivating example coming from two long pieces. Section 3.3 gives the nearby technical context that Kishino defeats some standard Alexander-biquandle-style detectors while being detected by other methods, which explains why the paper singles it out.
